transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-11
Start time: 16:32 PDT
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Priya Anand (Redwood SE), Tom Hale (Mariner VP Eng), Aisha Rahman (Mariner Cloud Architect), Diego Ramos (Mariner Network Eng)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on Mariner's requirements for a private VPC onramp. Primary concerns: regional data residency (EU/US split), egress/NAT policies, Transit Gateway vs PrivateLink, and whether Redwood Private can live in Mariner-managed account or needs Redwood-managed peering. Agreed to share peering template and follow up with a technical deep dive.

Topics covered:
- Current infra: multi-account AWS, Transit Gateway in use, strict egress controls
- Deployment modes: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (focus on Private)
- Networking: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, Transit Gateway, IP CIDR planning, route tables, security groups, NAT/egress, VPC endpoints
- Security/compliance: SOC 2, SAML SSO, KMS, audit logging
- Timeline and success criteria: POC in 4-6 weeks, <100ms median tail-latency target for inference, data never leaves customer VPC, support for EU region residency

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: All right everyone, thanks for hopping on. I think we have, uh, about 45-50 minutes. Quick intros? We'll mostly do discovery and then, Priya will jump into networking details.
[00:12] Tom Hale (Mariner): Tom here. Hi, VP of Eng at Mariner. We're mainly looking at moving inference out of our internal cluster and evaluating Redwood Private for per-tenant isolation.
[00:20] Aisha Rahman: Aisha, cloud architect. Focus on networking, regions, and compliance.
[00:26] Diego Ramos: Diego, network eng. I'll be digging into peering, TGW, NAT.
[00:31] Priya Anand: Priya, solutions eng on Redwood side, I'll talk through the private onramp options and material we can share.
[00:36] Lena: Cool. Tom, can you start with a quick context — what do you currently run for inference?
[00:44] Tom: Sure. Today we've got a kubernetes cluster on-prem for latency sensitive workloads, and a mix of EC2/GKE for batch stuff. We want to offload real-time text generation to a managed inference layer to reduce ops overhead. Important bit: some workloads process EU customer data and must stay in eu-west-1.
[01:05] Aisha: Also, we cannot have egress to public internet for certain models; all traffic must go through our NAT/IDS chain, and we want everything logged for audits.
[01:14] Lena: Got it. So data residency and egress controls are primary. Priya, quick overview of Private onramp?
[01:23] Priya: Yeah, the Private option lets you run Redwood control plane as a private service and connect the inference nodes via peering or PrivateLink. There are two common patterns: 1) Redwood-managed VPC with VPC peering or TGW attachments into your account, or 2) customer-managed deployment where Redwood software is deployed into your VPCs — we call that the Private deployment. Each has tradeoffs around ops ownership and network footprint.
[01:48] Diego: When you say Redwood-managed VPC, does that mean our traffic flows out to Redwood's account? We have a policy against cross-account egress for EU data.
[01:56] Priya: For EU-only data we can ensure inference nodes are in EU regions and we can route through PrivateLink so traffic never traverses the public internet — however we need to align on peering/Ingress egress policies. There are also options to deploy the inference nodes into your VPCs so nothing leaves your accounts, that removes the cross-account egress concern but increases customer ops responsibility.
[02:22] Tom: What's the difference between PrivateLink and Transit Gateway in your setup?
[02:26] Priya: Good question. PrivateLink (AWS NLB + interface endpoints) is better for per-service, per-region endpoints and works well with strict security. Transit Gateway is preferred when you want scaled routing between many VPCs and have existing TGW fabric — it's more complex but can be cleaner at scale. For a single-production VPC peering, direct VPC peering or TGW attachment both work. PrivateLink avoids route table changes in your VPCs.
[02:52] Aisha: We use TGW for most cross-account traffic already — attaching will simplify routes. But our TGW has strict propagation rules and we need to confirm Redwood's side supports TGW attachments in eu-west-1.
[03:04] Priya: We do support TGW attachments; we need your TGW id and the account id to propose the attachment. Alternatively, if you'd prefer PrivateLink we can provide NLB IPs and you create interface endpoints.
[03:18] Diego: About IP ranges — we maintain tight /22 ranges per environment. We need to avoid overlaps. Can you share what ranges Redwood uses?
[03:26] Lena: Yes, we'll send a peering template with suggested CIDRs. We'll also show example NAT and route tables.
[03:32] Tom: Also, how do you handle egress for model downloads and updates — do those come from the inference nodes or control plane? We have to make sure those downloads go through our approved proxy.
[03:42] Priya: Model artifacts are pulled by the inference nodes. If nodes are in your VPC they will follow your egress rules. If they are in Redwood-managed VPC, we can route artifact pulls through a customer-controlled S3 endpoint / VPC endpoint or set up a mirrored artifact repository in your account. We can also use signed pulls to satisfy audit requirements.
[04:04] Aisha: For compliance we'll need audit logs for inference requests and tokenization metadata — are those stored in Redwood logs or pushed into our logging stack?
[04:12] Priya: We can stream audit logs into your account — CloudWatch/Firehose to S3, or use our audit exports, depending on deployment. For Private deployments we typically push logs to your ELK/CloudWatch so nothing sensitive crosses accounts. There may be minimal control-plane telemetry that stays with Redwood for health monitoring but we can limit it.
[04:33] Lena: Question — are there any limits on concurrent connections or per-IP throughput for PrivateLink?
[04:38] Priya: AWS interface endpoints scale but you need to plan ENI counts and throughput — TGW attachments avoid ENI limits but you need TGW capacity. We'll help size based on your qps.
[04:50] Tom: Our target is 200 qps sustained with spikes to 400. Tail latency SLO is 100ms for 95th percentile ideally. Can Redwood meet that in a private deployment?
[05:02] Priya: We typically see <50ms median on modern GPU instances for small models; tail depends on model and sequence length. With colocated inference nodes in your region and KV cache warm-up, 100ms p95 is achievable. We'll need a POC to validate with your prompts.
[05:18] Diego: Do you support colocated instances in specific AZs? We have AZ affinity for our internal cache.
[05:24] Priya: Yes, we can provision in narrow AZs, but for redundancy we recommend multi-AZ. If AZ affinity is required, we can discuss single-AZ pinning for the initial POC.
[05:36] Aisha: Region-wise, our EU tenant data must stay in eu-west-1. US data in us-east-1. Can we have separate deployments per region and route from app stacks accordingly?
[05:47] Priya: Absolutely — multi-region Private deployments are common. You can pin models and versions per region. We'll need network connectivity and peering in each region, and a routing policy to ensure EU traffic hits eu-west-1 nodes.
[05:59] Tom: On encryption/KMS — can we bring our own keys for model encryption and for logging?
[06:05] Priya: For customer-managed deployments, BYOK options exist; we support KMS integrations. For Redwood-managed accounts we can use customer KMS via grants for certain artifacts. We'll map that out.
[06:16] Lena: Quick question about identity — SSO and RBAC integration?
[06:19] Priya: We support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning; RBAC roles can be mapped to your IdP groups. For private deployments you control access to the nodes and can enforce IAM restrictions.
[06:31] Diego: One more networking detail: our egress must pass through IDS that inspects outbound TLS. If inference nodes are in Redwood-managed account, will TLS be end-to-end to our proxy?
[06:42] Priya: We can terminate or proxy models through your endpoint — one pattern is to use a mirrored artifact repo in your account so nodes pull internally. For request traffic, if you want TLS inspection we can front with a proxy/forwarder in your VPC. We should map flow diagrams in the next call.
[06:58] Tom: Ok. On the commercial side, what's the lift to run Private vs Dedicated? We wanted predictable throughput but also minimal ops.
[07:06] Lena: Dedicated is Redwood-hosted reserved capacity in our infra but isolated to your account logically — lower ops for you but the nodes are in Redwood infrastructure. Private is full control in your VPC (or in your account with our package) — more ops but meets strict residency/compliance. We'll attach a short comparison doc after the call.
[07:25] Tom: Are there SLA differences?
[07:28] Priya: Dedicated comes with SLA commitments; Private can be SLA-backed in many enterprise contracts but depends on the deployment model and support tier.
[07:37] Aisha: For procurement we'll need SOC2 and ISO documents, plus a network security checklist.
[07:43] Lena: We'll send SOC2 and a network checklist.
[07:46] Diego: When you send the peering template, include required ports, security groups, and sample route table entries. Also we need to know if your NLB requires public IPs or if you can use internal NLBs.
[07:58] Priya: Internal NLBs are supported for PrivateLink; public IPs are not required. We'll include ports (gRPC/443 for inference, plus SSH/22 for ops if you opt in) and recommended SGs.
[08:12] Tom: How do you handle canary rollouts of model versions in a private deployment? We need safe rollouts.
[08:18] Priya: Rollouts can be controlled by your routing policy; we support canary traffic splitting, pinned versions per route, and automatic fallback to a stable variant. In private deployments you can run the control plane in a customer account to enforce policies.
[08:33] Aisha: We're also evaluating a hybrid — control plane in Redwood but inference nodes in our VPC. Does that work?
[08:38] Priya: Yes that's a common hybrid. It keeps control-plane ops with Redwood and places data plane in your account to satisfy compliance. We just need secure control-plane connectivity via private channels.
[08:50] Lena: Let's check scheduling — would next week work for a deeper technical session with your network team?
[08:55] Tom: Yeah, next week is fine. Prefer Wed or Thu.
[08:58] Aisha: Thu is better for our TGW team.
[09:01] Lena: Great. We'll schedule Thu 2025-08-14 10:00 UTC and invite Priya and our network SE.
[09:08] Diego: Quick note — we use an internal proxy for outbound TLS that does MITM inspection and re-encrypts to external services; we need to test if Redwood's TLS expectations break that.
[09:19] Priya: Noted — we'll include TLS-forwarding patterns and test scripts in the tech deep-dive.
[09:25] Tom: Any blockers from Redwood's side for TGW attach in eu-west-1? I just want to call that out.
[09:31] Priya: No blockers; we may need an IAM role and the TGW id. We'll share the minimal permissions.
[09:38] Lena: Ok, I'm going to summarize next steps — we'll send the peering template, SOC2/security pack, and propose the TGW attachment flow. Priya will prepare sizing.
[09:49] Tom: Perfect. A couple of quick questions from procurement — what's the approximate lead time for deploying in a customer-managed VPC?
[09:57] Priya: For POC it's typically 2-3 weeks if network approvals are quick. For production multi-region, plan 6-8 weeks. Depends on certs and audit windows.
[10:08] Aisha: For auditing we need all request logs for 90 days and the ability to export to our S3.
[10:13] Priya: That's supported — we'll include retention options.
[10:17] Diego: If we do TGW, we'll need BGP or static? We prefer static routes.
[10:22] Priya: Static is fine for peering; TGW attachments will usually use route tables with propagation, but we can design with static routes if that's your policy.
[10:32] Tom: On metrics, can we get token-level cost breakdowns per route or per API key? We want visibility for chargebacks.
[10:40] Priya: Yes, Redwood Console provides per-token and per-route cost/latency breakdowns. For private deployments we can forward telemetry into your monitoring stack too.
[10:48] Lena: Anything else anyone wants to raise?
[10:51] Tom: Just that we'll prioritize EU tenancy first, then roll US. Also license review once procurement sees the contract.
[10:58] Aisha: We'll also share a short list of compliance questions via email; please assign a contact for security.
[11:05] Lena: I'll be primary. Priya will be SE contact.
[11:08] Priya: Sounds good. We'll also prep a short benchmark plan — sample prompts, expected qps, and latency measurement scripts.
[11:18] Diego: Can you also include recommended instance types and memory footprint per model?
[11:22] Priya: Yep, we'll include model profiles.
[11:25] Tom: Great. If we can get the peering template and SOC2 this week, procurement will start their paperwork.
[11:32] Lena: We'll target end of day 2025-08-13 for the docs.
[11:36] Tom: Ok thanks everyone.
[11:38] Lena: Thanks, talk soon.

End of call.
